screens.title: Ansible's Agentless Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible stands out as a leading automation engine, largely due to its elegant agentless architecture. Unlike many other automation tools that demand a software agent to be installed and maintained on every managed device, Ansible operates differently. It connects to your network devices, servers, or cloud instances using standard, secure protocols that are already present. For network devices, this typically means SSH, while for Windows machines, it might be WinRM. This fundamental design choice significantly reduces the operational overhead. You don't need to worry about deploying, updating, or troubleshooting agents across your infrastructure. Instead, your focus shifts entirely to writing the automation logic. The Control Node, which is your workstation or a dedicated server, acts as the central point from which all automation tasks are initiated. It communicates securely with the Managed Nodes, which are the target devices you want to automate. This streamlined approach makes Ansible incredibly easy to deploy and manage, allowing you to quickly start automating without complex prerequisites. This agentless nature is a major advantage, simplifying your setup and accelerating your path to network automation. Ansible's Agentless Architecture means ansible's agentless architecture uses standard protocols like ssh, eliminating the need for agents on managed nodes and simplifying deployment and management.. In practical terms, discover how ansible manages devices without requiring any software installation on them.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: The Ansible Inventory: Defining Your Network
screens.narratorSegment: The Ansible Inventory is the cornerstone of any automation project, serving as a comprehensive list of all the managed nodes that Ansible will interact with. Think of it as your network's address book, detailing every device you intend to automate. This file, or collection of files, not only lists the devices but also organizes them into logical groups, such as 'routers,' 'switches,' or 'data_center_a.' This grouping is incredibly powerful, allowing you to target specific sets of devices with your automation tasks. For example, you might want to apply a configuration only to all your core routers, and the inventory makes this selection straightforward. Beyond just listing devices, the inventory also stores variables specific to those nodes or groups. These variables can include connection types, credentials, or device-specific parameters like the network operating system, such as ansible underscore network underscore os. ios. Inventories can be static, like a simple text file you manually create, or dynamic, generated on the fly from cloud providers or configuration management databases. The flexibility of the inventory ensures that your automation can adapt to diverse and evolving network topologies. A common mistake is hardcoding sensitive credentials directly into the inventory; always use Ansible Vault for security.

screens.title: Crafting Your First Inventory File
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating a practical Ansible inventory file, which is typically named inventory. ini. This file uses a simple INI-like format to define your managed nodes and their properties. As you can see in the example, we start by defining groups using square brackets, like open square bracket routers close square bracket and open square bracket switches close square bracket. Within each group, you list the hostnames or IP addresses of your devices. For each device, you can specify host-specific variables. For instance, router1. example. com is assigned ansible underscore host equals 192.168.1.1, ansible underscore user equals admin, and ansible underscore password equals cisco. The ansible underscore network underscore os equals ios variable is crucial for network devices, telling Ansible which operating system to expect, enabling it to use the correct network modules. Below the device definitions, we have the open square bracket all. vars close square bracket section. This is where you define variables that apply to all hosts in your inventory. Here, ansible underscore connection equals network underscore cli specifies the connection plugin for network devices, and ansible underscore become equals yes along with ansible underscore become underscore method equals enable and ansible underscore become underscore pass equals cisco are used for privilege escalation, similar to using enable mode on a Cisco device. Remember the common mistake: never hardcode sensitive credentials like passwords directly in this file for production environments. Always use Ansible Vault, which we'll cover shortly, to encrypt such data. This structured approach ensures clarity and maintainability for your automation projects.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Crafting Your First Inventory File
Code Walkthrough

Crafting Your First Inventory File

Explore the structure of a basic inventory.ini file for network devices.

Groups & Hosts

Devices are organized into groups (e.g., [routers]) with individual host entries.

Host Variables

Each host can have specific variables like ansible_host, ansible_user, and ansible_network_os.

Global Variables

The [all:vars] section defines variables that apply to all managed nodes, such as connection type and privilege escalation.

Common Mistake

Hardcoding sensitive credentials directly in the inventory. Always use Ansible Vault for passwords and API keys.

inventory.iniYAML
# inventory.ini

[routers]
router1.example.com ansible_host=192.168.1.1 ansible_user=admin ansible_password=cisco ansible_network_os=ios
router2.example.com ansible_host=192.168.1.2 ansible_user=admin ansible_password=cisco ansible_network_os=ios

[switches]
switch1.example.com ansible_host=192.168.1.10 ansible_user=admin ansible_password=cisco ansible_network_os=ios
switch2.example.com ansible_host=192.168.1.11 ansible_user=admin ansible_password=cisco ansible_network_os=ios

[all:vars]
ansible_connection=network_cli
ansible_become=yes
ansible_become_method=enable
ansible_become_pass=cisco

screens.title: Playbooks: The Heart of Ansible Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Playbooks are truly the heart of Ansible automation, serving as the blueprint for all your automated tasks. Written in YAML, a human-readable data serialization standard, playbooks describe the desired state of your managed nodes or a series of tasks to be executed. Each playbook is composed of one or more 'plays,' and each play targets a specific group of hosts that you've defined in your inventory. This allows for granular control, ensuring that the right automation runs on the right devices. Within each play, you define a list of 'tasks.' A task is a single action that Ansible performs, and it always calls an Ansible Module. Modules are reusable units of code that perform specific actions, such as configuring an interface, creating a file, or starting a service. Ansible provides an extensive collection of modules, including specialized network modules for various vendors like Cisco IOS, IOS-XE, and NX-OS. These network modules are often designed with idempotency in mind, meaning you can run the same playbook multiple times, and it will only make changes if the desired state is not already met. This simplifies your playbook logic and prevents unintended reconfigurations. Understanding the structure of playbooks and the role of modules is fundamental to building effective and reliable network automation solutions.

screens.title: Configuring VLANs with an Ansible Playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Let's put our knowledge into practice by examining a simple yet powerful Ansible playbook designed to configure a VLAN on Cisco IOS-XE switches. This playbook, named configure underscore vlan. yml, begins with ---, a standard YAML document separator. The name field provides a human-readable description of the playbook's purpose. Crucially, hosts. switches tells Ansible to execute this playbook only on the devices defined in the 'switches' group within our inventory. We set gather underscore facts. no to speed up execution, as we don't need to collect extensive information about the devices for this simple configuration. The connection. network underscore cli specifies the connection method. Within the tasks section, we define a single task: 'Ensure VLAN 100 exists and is named 'Automation_VLAN'.' This task calls the cisco. ios. ios underscore vlan module, a specialized network module for Cisco IOS devices. We provide vlan underscore id. 100 and name. Automation underscore VLAN as parameters, and state. present ensures that the VLAN is created or updated to match this desired state. The register. vlan underscore result captures the output of this task, which we then use in a debug task to print whether a change was made. This example clearly demonstrates how a playbook orchestrates tasks using specific modules to achieve a desired network configuration. The state. present parameter is key to its idempotency. If VLAN 100 already exists with the name 'Automation_VLAN', the module will report no changes. If it doesn't exist or has a different name, it will apply the necessary configuration.

keyIdea.title: Idempotent VLAN Configuration
keyIdea.text: A playbook uses the `cisco.ios.ios_vlan` module with `state: present` to ensure a VLAN exists with a specific ID and name, applying changes only if necessary.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Configuring VLANs with Ansible
Practical Example

Configuring VLANs with an Ansible Playbook

Walk through a playbook that uses the ios_vlan module to manage VLANs on Cisco IOS-XE.

Targeting Hosts

The hosts: switches directive ensures the playbook runs only on devices in the 'switches' group.

Using `ios_vlan` Module

The cisco.ios.ios_vlan module is used to ensure VLAN 100 exists with the name 'Automation_VLAN' and state: present.

Key Takeaway

Ansible playbooks leverage specific network modules like ios_vlan to declaratively configure network devices, ensuring idempotency and simplifying complex tasks.

configure_vlan.ymlYAML
# configure_vlan.yml
---
- name: Configure VLAN on Cisco IOS-XE switches
  hosts: switches # Targets the 'switches' group from inventory.ini
  gather_facts: no # Not needed for simple config, speeds up execution
  connection: network_cli

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure VLAN 100 exists and is named 'Automation_VLAN'
      cisco.ios.ios_vlan:
        vlan_id: 100
        name: Automation_VLAN
        state: present # Ensures the VLAN exists
      register: vlan_result

    - name: Print VLAN configuration status
      debug:
        msg: "VLAN 100 configuration status: {{ vlan_result.changed }}"

screens.title: Running Playbooks and Understanding Idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've crafted your Ansible playbook, the next step is to execute it. You run a playbook using the ansible-playbook command, specifying your inventory file with the -i flag and the playbook file itself. For our VLAN configuration example, the command would be ansible-playbook -i inventory. ini configure underscore vlan. yml. When this command runs, Ansible connects to the target devices, reads the tasks defined in the playbook, and executes them using the appropriate modules. A key concept in Ansible, especially with network modules, is idempotency. This means that running the same playbook multiple times will produce the same result without causing unintended side effects. If the desired state is already achieved, Ansible will report 'ok' and make no changes. If the device's configuration doesn't match the desired state, Ansible will apply the necessary changes and report 'changed.' For example, with our ios underscore vlan module and state. present, if VLAN 100 already exists with the name 'Automation_VLAN', the module will detect this and report no changes. If it's missing or has a different name, it will configure it. This idempotent behavior is incredibly valuable in automation, as it allows you to safely re-run playbooks without worrying about breaking existing configurations, ensuring consistency and reliability across your network infrastructure. It simplifies your automation logic significantly, as you don't need to write complex conditional checks to determine if a configuration already exists.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Running Playbooks & Idempotency
Execution & Idempotency

Running Playbooks and Understanding Idempotency

Learn how to execute an Ansible playbook and the importance of idempotent design.

Executing Playbooks

Use the ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini your_playbook.yml command to run your automation.

Idempotency Principle

Running a playbook multiple times yields the same result; changes are only applied if the desired state is not already met.

Key Takeaway

Idempotency is a core strength of Ansible, allowing safe and repeatable execution of playbooks without fear of unintended side effects or reconfigurations.

Terminal OutputBash
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini configure_vlan.yml

PLAY [Configure VLAN on Cisco IOS-XE switches] *********************************

TASK [Ensure VLAN 100 exists and is named 'Automation_VLAN'] *******************
changed: [switch1.example.com]
ok: [switch2.example.com]

TASK [Print VLAN configuration status] *****************************************
ok: [switch1.example.com] => {
    "msg": "VLAN 100 configuration status: True"
}
ok: [switch2.example.com] => {
    "msg": "VLAN 100 configuration status: False"
}

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
switch1.example.com : ok=2   changed=1   unreachable=0   failed=0   skipped=0   rescued=0   ignored=0
switch2.example.com : ok=2   changed=0   unreachable=0   failed=0   skipped=0   rescued=0   ignored=0

screens.title: Exploring Specialized Network Modules
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible's power for network automation is greatly enhanced by its rich ecosystem of specialized network modules. While we've seen cisco. ios. ios underscore vlan for VLAN management, there are many others designed for specific configuration tasks. For instance, cisco. ios. ios underscore interfaces is a versatile module for managing interface settings, allowing you to configure descriptions, enable/disable interfaces, and set various parameters. Similarly, cisco. ios. ios underscore static underscore routes helps automate the configuration of static routes on your devices. These modules abstract away the underlying CLI commands, allowing you to focus on the desired state rather than the command syntax. They also often incorporate idempotency, ensuring that configurations are applied intelligently. However, there might be scenarios where a specific module for a particular configuration isn't available. In such cases, the cisco. ios. ios underscore config module becomes invaluable. This powerful module allows you to send raw CLI commands directly to the device. While flexible, it's important to note that using ios underscore config means you lose some of the built-in idempotency and error checking that higher-level modules offer. Therefore, the best practice is always to prioritize using specific network modules when they are available, as they provide a more robust, idempotent, and maintainable approach to network automation. This strategic choice simplifies your playbooks and reduces the potential for configuration errors.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Exploring Specialized Network Modules
Network Modules

Exploring Specialized Network Modules

Discover various Ansible modules for comprehensive network device configuration.

Specific Modules

Modules like cisco.ios.ios_interfaces and cisco.ios.ios_static_routes provide high-level, idempotent control over specific configurations.

`ios_config` Module

A powerful module for sending raw CLI commands when a specific, higher-level module is not available.

Key Takeaway

Prioritize using specific network modules for their idempotency and abstraction, reserving ios_config for unique or unsupported CLI commands.

Common Network Modules
ios_vlan

Manages VLAN IDs and names.

ios_interfaces

Configures interface settings (description, state).

ios_static_routes

Manages static routing entries.

ios_config

Executes arbitrary CLI commands.

Pro Tip

Always check Ansible documentation for vendor-specific modules before resorting to raw CLI commands with ios_config.

screens.title: Securing Sensitive Data with Ansible Vault
screens.narratorSegment: In any automation solution, securing sensitive data is absolutely paramount. This is especially true in network automation, where you're often dealing with device credentials, A P I keys, and other confidential information. Storing these in plain text within your playbooks or inventory files is a significant security risk. This is where Ansible Vault comes in. Ansible Vault provides a robust way to encrypt variables, entire files, or even whole playbooks, ensuring that your sensitive data is protected. When you encrypt data with Ansible Vault, it becomes unreadable without the correct vault password. This means you can safely store your Ansible projects in version control systems like Git without exposing your credentials. You can encrypt individual variables directly within a playbook, or, more commonly, encrypt an entire YAML file, such as a vars slash secret underscore vars. yml file that holds all your sensitive variables. When Ansible needs to access vaulted data during a playbook run, it will prompt you for the vault password. This integrates seamlessly into your workflow, allowing you to maintain strong security practices without hindering your automation efforts. By mastering Ansible Vault, you add a critical layer of security to your network automation solutions, protecting your infrastructure from unauthorized access. This is not just a good practice, but a critical requirement for production environments.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Securing Data with Ansible Vault
Security Best Practice

Securing Sensitive Data with Ansible Vault

Learn how to encrypt credentials and other confidential information in your Ansible projects.

Encryption for Security

Encrypts variables, files, or entire playbooks to protect sensitive data like passwords and API keys.

Seamless Integration

Integrates into your workflow by prompting for a vault password when accessing encrypted data.

Key Takeaway

Ansible Vault is essential for securing sensitive information, enabling safe storage and use of credentials in automation projects.

Terminal CommandsBash
# Encrypt an existing file
ansible-vault encrypt secret_vars.yml

# Create a new encrypted file
ansible-vault create new_secret.yml

# Edit an existing encrypted file
ansible-vault edit secret_vars.yml

# Run playbook with vaulted data
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini configure_vlan.yml --ask-vault-pass
# OR
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini configure_vlan.yml --vault-password-file vault_pass.txt

screens.title: Automating Interface Configuration with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's apply what we've learned to a more complex scenario: automating the configuration of multiple interfaces on a Cisco IOS-XE router. This task is common in network deployments and perfectly suited for Ansible. We'll use the cisco. ios. ios underscore interfaces module, which is designed to manage interface settings efficiently. As you can see in the playbook, we define a config block that contains a list of interfaces to configure. For each interface, like Gigabit Ethernet1 and Gigabit Ethernet2, we specify its name, a descriptive description, and set enabled. true to ensure it's administratively up. The state. merged parameter is crucial here; it tells Ansible to merge these configurations with any existing ones on the device, rather than replacing them entirely. This ensures that only the specified parameters are changed, preserving other interface settings. After configuring the interfaces, we include debug tasks to print the status of each interface, showing whether changes were applied. Finally, a critical step in network automation is to save the configuration. The cisco. ios. ios underscore config module with save underscore when. modified ensures that the running configuration is saved to startup configuration only if changes were made. This comprehensive example demonstrates how to use a single playbook to manage multiple interface configurations, ensuring consistency and reducing manual effort. This approach is far more reliable and scalable than manual CLI commands, especially when dealing with many devices or interfaces.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Automating Interface Configuration
Advanced Application

Automating Interface Configuration with Ansible

Apply your knowledge to configure multiple interfaces on a Cisco IOS-XE router.

`ios_interfaces` Module

Used to configure interface properties like description and administrative state (enabled: true).

`state: merged`

Ensures that specified configurations are merged with existing ones, preventing unintended overwrites.

Saving Configuration

The `ios_config` module with `save_when: modified` ensures changes are persisted only if applied.

Key Takeaway

Automating interface configurations with Ansible provides a scalable, consistent, and error-resistant method for managing network device settings.

configure_interfaces.ymlYAML
---
- name: Configure interfaces on Cisco IOS-XE routers
  hosts: routers
  gather_facts: no
  connection: network_cli

  tasks:
    - name: Configure GigabitEthernet1
      cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
        config:
          - name: GigabitEthernet1
            description: "Uplink to Core"
            enabled: true
        state: merged
      register: interface1_result

    - name: Configure GigabitEthernet2
      cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
        config:
          - name: GigabitEthernet2
            description: "Connects to Servers"
            enabled: true
        state: merged
      register: interface2_result

    - name: Save configuration
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: modified

screens.title: Key Concepts: Ansible Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: As we conclude our exploration of Ansible, let's recap some of the fundamental concepts that are crucial for effective network automation. First, remember the Ansible Control Node: this is the machine where Ansible is installed and from which all your playbooks are executed. It's the brain of your automation setup. Second, we have the Ansible Managed Node, which refers to the target device, whether it's a network device, server, or cloud instance, that Ansible manages. The beauty here is that no agent software is needed on these nodes. Third, the Inventory is your comprehensive list of managed nodes, organized into groups with specific variables. It's how Ansible knows what devices to talk to and how to connect. Understanding these three components provides a solid foundation for building and deploying your automation solutions. They work together to create a powerful and flexible framework for managing your network infrastructure. Keep these definitions clear as you move forward with your automation journey.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Key Concepts: Fundamentals

Key Concepts: Ansible Fundamentals

Reinforce your understanding of Ansible's core components for network automation.

Control Node

The machine where Ansible is installed and from which playbooks are executed.

Managed Node

The target device (network device, server, etc.) that Ansible manages, requiring no agent.

Inventory

A file that defines managed nodes, organizes them into groups, and provides variables.

Summary Takeaway

Ansible's agentless architecture, driven by a Control Node interacting with Managed Nodes defined in an Inventory, forms the foundation for efficient network automation.

screens.title: Key Concepts: Automation Workflow & Security
screens.narratorSegment: Let's continue our review with the key concepts that drive Ansible's automation workflow and ensure its security. First, Playbooks are YAML files that describe the desired state or a series of tasks to be executed on your managed nodes. They are the scripts that bring your automation to life. Second, Ansible Modules are reusable units of code that perform specific actions on a managed node, such as configuring a VLAN or an interface. These modules abstract away complex CLI commands and often provide idempotency, making your automation reliable. Finally, Ansible Vault is a critical security feature used to encrypt sensitive data, like passwords and A P I keys, within your Ansible projects. This protects confidential information from being exposed in plain text, which is essential for maintaining a secure automation environment. Together, these concepts empower you to build robust, efficient, and secure network automation solutions. By understanding how playbooks orchestrate tasks using modules and how Vault protects your sensitive data, you are well-equipped to tackle real-world automation challenges.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to Chapter 6.2, where we'll dive into implementing network automation using Ansible. In today's complex network environments, manual configuration is not only time-consuming but also prone to errors. Ansible offers a robust, open-source solution to automate these tasks, making your network operations more efficient and reliable. You'll learn how Ansible's agentless architecture simplifies deployment, allowing you to focus on defining the desired state of your network rather than managing agents on each device. This chapter will equip you with the foundational knowledge to leverage Ansible for configuring Cisco IOS-XE devices, from understanding its core components to securing sensitive data. By the end, you'll be able to write and execute basic playbooks, transforming the way you manage network infrastructure. Let's explore how Ansible can revolutionize your approach to network automation.

In this chapter, we'll set out to achieve several key learning objectives that will empower you to effectively use Ansible for network automation. First, you will learn to explain the core components of Ansible, such as the Control Node, Managed Nodes, Inventory, Playbooks, and Modules. Understanding these fundamental building blocks is crucial for grasping how Ansible operates and interacts with your network devices. For example, knowing the role of the Control Node helps you understand where your automation scripts run from. Second, you will develop the skill to create an Ansible inventory file, which is essential for defining and organizing your network devices and groups. This allows you to target specific sets of devices for automation tasks, ensuring your configurations are applied precisely where needed. These objectives lay the groundwork for practical automation, enabling you to manage your network infrastructure with greater precision and efficiency.

Continuing our journey, the next set of objectives focuses on the practical application of Ansible. You will learn to write basic Ansible playbooks, which are essentially the scripts that tell Ansible what tasks to perform on your network devices. This includes understanding the YAML syntax and how to structure a playbook for configuration tasks on Cisco IOS-XE devices. For instance, you'll see how to define a series of steps to achieve a desired network state. Furthermore, you'll gain proficiency in utilizing common Ansible network modules. These modules are pre-built tools designed to handle specific network tasks, such as configuring interfaces or managing VLANs, significantly simplifying your automation efforts. Finally, a critical objective is to implement Ansible Vault to secure sensitive data within your playbooks and inventory. This ensures that credentials and other confidential information are protected, which is paramount for maintaining security in any automation solution. These objectives will enable you to build secure, effective, and scalable network automation solutions.

Ansible stands out as a leading automation engine, largely due to its elegant agentless architecture. Unlike many other automation tools that demand a software agent to be installed and maintained on every managed device, Ansible operates differently. It connects to your network devices, servers, or cloud instances using standard, secure protocols that are already present. For network devices, this typically means SSH, while for Windows machines, it might be WinRM. This fundamental design choice significantly reduces the operational overhead. You don't need to worry about deploying, updating, or troubleshooting agents across your infrastructure. Instead, your focus shifts entirely to writing the automation logic. The Control Node, which is your workstation or a dedicated server, acts as the central point from which all automation tasks are initiated. It communicates securely with the Managed Nodes, which are the target devices you want to automate. This streamlined approach makes Ansible incredibly easy to deploy and manage, allowing you to quickly start automating without complex prerequisites. This agentless nature is a major advantage, simplifying your setup and accelerating your path to network automation. Ansible's Agentless Architecture means ansible's agentless architecture uses standard protocols like ssh, eliminating the need for agents on managed nodes and simplifying deployment and management.. In practical terms, discover how ansible manages devices without requiring any software installation on them.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Ansible Inventory is the cornerstone of any automation project, serving as a comprehensive list of all the managed nodes that Ansible will interact with. Think of it as your network's address book, detailing every device you intend to automate. This file, or collection of files, not only lists the devices but also organizes them into logical groups, such as 'routers,' 'switches,' or 'data_center_a.' This grouping is incredibly powerful, allowing you to target specific sets of devices with your automation tasks. For example, you might want to apply a configuration only to all your core routers, and the inventory makes this selection straightforward. Beyond just listing devices, the inventory also stores variables specific to those nodes or groups. These variables can include connection types, credentials, or device-specific parameters like the network operating system, such as ansible underscore network underscore os. ios. Inventories can be static, like a simple text file you manually create, or dynamic, generated on the fly from cloud providers or configuration management databases. The flexibility of the inventory ensures that your automation can adapt to diverse and evolving network topologies. A common mistake is hardcoding sensitive credentials directly into the inventory; always use Ansible Vault for security.

Let's walk through creating a practical Ansible inventory file, which is typically named inventory. ini. This file uses a simple INI-like format to define your managed nodes and their properties. As you can see in the example, we start by defining groups using square brackets, like open square bracket routers close square bracket and open square bracket switches close square bracket. Within each group, you list the hostnames or IP addresses of your devices. For each device, you can specify host-specific variables. For instance, router1. example. com is assigned ansible underscore host equals 192.168.1.1, ansible underscore user equals admin, and ansible underscore password equals cisco. The ansible underscore network underscore os equals ios variable is crucial for network devices, telling Ansible which operating system to expect, enabling it to use the correct network modules. Below the device definitions, we have the open square bracket all. vars close square bracket section. This is where you define variables that apply to all hosts in your inventory. Here, ansible underscore connection equals network underscore cli specifies the connection plugin for network devices, and ansible underscore become equals yes along with ansible underscore become underscore method equals enable and ansible underscore become underscore pass equals cisco are used for privilege escalation, similar to using enable mode on a Cisco device. Remember the common mistake: never hardcode sensitive credentials like passwords directly in this file for production environments. Always use Ansible Vault, which we'll cover shortly, to encrypt such data. This structured approach ensures clarity and maintainability for your automation projects.

Playbooks are truly the heart of Ansible automation, serving as the blueprint for all your automated tasks. Written in YAML, a human-readable data serialization standard, playbooks describe the desired state of your managed nodes or a series of tasks to be executed. Each playbook is composed of one or more 'plays,' and each play targets a specific group of hosts that you've defined in your inventory. This allows for granular control, ensuring that the right automation runs on the right devices. Within each play, you define a list of 'tasks.' A task is a single action that Ansible performs, and it always calls an Ansible Module. Modules are reusable units of code that perform specific actions, such as configuring an interface, creating a file, or starting a service. Ansible provides an extensive collection of modules, including specialized network modules for various vendors like Cisco IOS, IOS-XE, and NX-OS. These network modules are often designed with idempotency in mind, meaning you can run the same playbook multiple times, and it will only make changes if the desired state is not already met. This simplifies your playbook logic and prevents unintended reconfigurations. Understanding the structure of playbooks and the role of modules is fundamental to building effective and reliable network automation solutions.

Let's put our knowledge into practice by examining a simple yet powerful Ansible playbook designed to configure a VLAN on Cisco IOS-XE switches. This playbook, named configure underscore vlan. yml, begins with ---, a standard YAML document separator. The name field provides a human-readable description of the playbook's purpose. Crucially, hosts. switches tells Ansible to execute this playbook only on the devices defined in the 'switches' group within our inventory. We set gather underscore facts. no to speed up execution, as we don't need to collect extensive information about the devices for this simple configuration. The connection. network underscore cli specifies the connection method. Within the tasks section, we define a single task: 'Ensure VLAN 100 exists and is named 'Automation_VLAN'.' This task calls the cisco. ios. ios underscore vlan module, a specialized network module for Cisco IOS devices. We provide vlan underscore id. 100 and name. Automation underscore VLAN as parameters, and state. present ensures that the VLAN is created or updated to match this desired state. The register. vlan underscore result captures the output of this task, which we then use in a debug task to print whether a change was made. This example clearly demonstrates how a playbook orchestrates tasks using specific modules to achieve a desired network configuration. The state. present parameter is key to its idempotency. If VLAN 100 already exists with the name 'Automation_VLAN', the module will report no changes. If it doesn't exist or has a different name, it will apply the necessary configuration.

Once you've crafted your Ansible playbook, the next step is to execute it. You run a playbook using the ansible-playbook command, specifying your inventory file with the -i flag and the playbook file itself. For our VLAN configuration example, the command would be ansible-playbook -i inventory. ini configure underscore vlan. yml. When this command runs, Ansible connects to the target devices, reads the tasks defined in the playbook, and executes them using the appropriate modules. A key concept in Ansible, especially with network modules, is idempotency. This means that running the same playbook multiple times will produce the same result without causing unintended side effects. If the desired state is already achieved, Ansible will report 'ok' and make no changes. If the device's configuration doesn't match the desired state, Ansible will apply the necessary changes and report 'changed.' For example, with our ios underscore vlan module and state. present, if VLAN 100 already exists with the name 'Automation_VLAN', the module will detect this and report no changes. If it's missing or has a different name, it will configure it. This idempotent behavior is incredibly valuable in automation, as it allows you to safely re-run playbooks without worrying about breaking existing configurations, ensuring consistency and reliability across your network infrastructure. It simplifies your automation logic significantly, as you don't need to write complex conditional checks to determine if a configuration already exists.

Ansible's power for network automation is greatly enhanced by its rich ecosystem of specialized network modules. While we've seen cisco. ios. ios underscore vlan for VLAN management, there are many others designed for specific configuration tasks. For instance, cisco. ios. ios underscore interfaces is a versatile module for managing interface settings, allowing you to configure descriptions, enable/disable interfaces, and set various parameters. Similarly, cisco. ios. ios underscore static underscore routes helps automate the configuration of static routes on your devices. This powerful module allows you to send raw CLI commands directly to the device. While flexible, it's important to note that using ios underscore config means you lose some of the built-in idempotency and error checking that higher-level modules offer. Therefore, the best practice is always to prioritize using specific network modules when they are available, as they provide a more robust, idempotent, and maintainable approach to network automation. This strategic choice simplifies your playbooks and reduces the potential for configuration errors.

This is especially true in network automation, where you're often dealing with device credentials, A P I keys, and other confidential information. Storing these in plain text within your playbooks or inventory files is a significant security risk. This is where Ansible Vault comes in. Ansible Vault provides a robust way to encrypt variables, entire files, or even whole playbooks, ensuring that your sensitive data is protected. This is not just a good practice, but a critical requirement for production environments.

Now, let's apply what we've learned to a more complex scenario: automating the configuration of multiple interfaces on a Cisco IOS-XE router. This task is common in network deployments and perfectly suited for Ansible. We'll use the cisco. ios. ios underscore interfaces module, which is designed to manage interface settings efficiently. As you can see in the playbook, we define a config block that contains a list of interfaces to configure. For each interface, like Gigabit Ethernet1 and Gigabit Ethernet2, we specify its name, a descriptive description, and set enabled. true to ensure it's administratively up. The state. merged parameter is crucial here; it tells Ansible to merge these configurations with any existing ones on the device, rather than replacing them entirely. This ensures that only the specified parameters are changed, preserving other interface settings. After configuring the interfaces, we include debug tasks to print the status of each interface, showing whether changes were applied. Finally, a critical step in network automation is to save the configuration. The cisco. ios. ios underscore config module with save underscore when. modified ensures that the running configuration is saved to startup configuration only if changes were made. This comprehensive example demonstrates how to use a single playbook to manage multiple interface configurations, ensuring consistency and reducing manual effort. This approach is far more reliable and scalable than manual CLI commands, especially when dealing with many devices or interfaces.

As we conclude our exploration of Ansible, let's recap some of the fundamental concepts that are crucial for effective network automation. First, remember the Ansible Control Node: this is the machine where Ansible is installed and from which all your playbooks are executed. It's the brain of your automation setup. Second, we have the Ansible Managed Node, which refers to the target device, whether it's a network device, server, or cloud instance, that Ansible manages. The beauty here is that no agent software is needed on these nodes. Third, the Inventory is your comprehensive list of managed nodes, organized into groups with specific variables. It's how Ansible knows what devices to talk to and how to connect. Understanding these three components provides a solid foundation for building and deploying your automation solutions. They work together to create a powerful and flexible framework for managing your network infrastructure. Keep these definitions clear as you move forward with your automation journey.

Let's continue our review with the key concepts that drive Ansible's automation workflow and ensure its security. First, Playbooks are YAML files that describe the desired state or a series of tasks to be executed on your managed nodes. They are the scripts that bring your automation to life. Second, Ansible Modules are reusable units of code that perform specific actions on a managed node, such as configuring a VLAN or an interface. These modules abstract away complex CLI commands and often provide idempotency, making your automation reliable. Finally, Ansible Vault is a critical security feature used to encrypt sensitive data, like passwords and A P I keys, within your Ansible projects. This protects confidential information from being exposed in plain text, which is essential for maintaining a secure automation environment. Together, these concepts empower you to build robust, efficient, and secure network automation solutions. By understanding how playbooks orchestrate tasks using modules and how Vault protects your sensitive data, you are well-equipped to tackle real-world automation challenges.
